description: NAKSHATRA X is a Jaipur-based team at NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, working on Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map. We're exploring how geospatial data, elevation models and interactive maps can support terrain-aware route planning on Mars. Our interests include software engineering, Python, GIS and data visualization. We welcome teammates skilled in GIS/remote sensing, web development, UI/UX, planetary science or storytelling. We value curiosity, collaboration and scientific accuracy.
summary:
VyomPath is an interactive Mars terrain-exploration and traverse decision-support workspace built for NASA Space Apps Challenge's Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map. Users explore planetary map layers, draw alternative rover traverses, and inspect distance, elevation, slope, and terrain-data coverage.

Its flagship feature, Mission-Aware Traverse Intelligence, evaluates routes under three selectable priorities: slope-conscious, energy-efficient, and data-confidence-first. It combines measured route metrics using documented weighted scoring and explains the trade-offs behind each result.

The local analysis workflow samples a high-resolution HiRISE Jezero Crater DTM at approximately 1.01 metres per pixel, while preserving NoData gaps and out-of-bounds coverage. The public hosted demonstration currently uses clearly identified synthetic data because the real DTM is not mounted on its backend; real raster-backed analysis is available in the local setup. VyomPath is an exploratory planning prototype, not a rover-safety certification system.
details:
What is VyomPath?

VyomPath is an interactive Martian terrain-exploration and traverse decision-support workspace developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 by Team NAKSHATRA X.

It allows users to explore Mars, draw potential rover traverses, inspect terrain characteristics, and compare alternative routes using elevation, slope, distance, and terrain-data coverage.

Its central differentiator is Mission-Aware Traverse Intelligence: instead of only displaying terrain measurements, VyomPath evaluates alternative routes according to the priorities of a particular exploration mission.

How it works

VyomPath combines three connected capabilities.

1. Planetary map visualization

The frontend uses React, TypeScript and OpenLayers to display interactive Mars maps. Users can explore MOLA shaded relief, CTX imagery and Viking MDIM 2.1, draw traverses, inspect overlays and compare potential routes.

2. Numerical terrain analysis

A Python FastAPI backend receives route coordinates and performs geospatial analysis. When a valid local HiRISE Float32 Digital Terrain Model is configured, the terrain engine samples elevation values, generates elevation profiles, calculates slope characteristics and evaluates valid-data coverage.

The local workflow uses the HiRISE stereo DTM product DTEEC_023524_1985_023379_1985_U01, with approximately 1.01 metres per pixel posting.

The application handles NoData values, partial coverage and out-of-bounds routes instead of silently treating missing elevation measurements as valid terrain.

3. Mission-Aware Traverse Intelligence — Our USP

Conventional terrain viewers help users see a route's elevation and slope. VyomPath adds an explainable, mission-specific comparison of alternative traverses.

Users can select one of three mission objectives:

Slope-Conscious Traverse

Prioritizes lower maximum and average slopes, fewer steep terrain segments and better terrain-data coverage.

Energy-Efficient Traverse

Prioritizes shorter distances, lower cumulative elevation gain and a lower estimated mechanical-work requirement.

Data-Confidence-First Traverse

Prioritizes valid HiRISE DTM coverage and penalizes NoData gaps and routes extending beyond the available terrain dataset.

For each route, the engine calculates normalized scores for slope, energy and data confidence. These are combined using objective-specific weights:

The feature displays overall scores, individual metric contributions, advantages, disadvantages and an explanation grounded in measured route differences.

It also avoids overstating small differences: routes scoring within two points are identified as a tie or near-parity rather than producing an exaggerated recommendation. When only one route is available, it provides an individual assessment instead of pretending a comparison exists.

The energy calculation includes a simplified mechanical-work proxy using reference rover mass, Martian gravity and an assumed rolling-resistance coefficient. It is an estimate, not measured battery consumption or a validated rover power model.

The result is a transparent decision-support workflow that helps users understand how their preferred route changes when mission priorities change.

Scientific approach and data integrity

A central design decision is separating visual map imagery from numerical terrain analysis. A rendered map tile is never treated as an elevation measurement.

The local terrain-analysis workflow samples the HiRISE DTM directly. Missing raster values remain missing; partial coverage and out-of-bounds routes are communicated explicitly.

VyomPath also distinguishes real DTM analysis from synthetic demonstration data. It does not label a route as safe or flight-certified. Orbital terrain models cannot independently resolve every sub-pixel obstacle, soil property or rover mobility hazard.

The scoring thresholds and objective weights are prototype decision-support assumptions, not universally validated rover mobility limits. The 15° steep-segment threshold and 30° maximum-slope normalization reference are heuristic scoring values. The energy assessment uses a simplified mechanical-work proxy with assumed reference rover mass and rolling resistance; it does not calculate actual battery consumption or certify rover mobility. All recommendations must be interpreted alongside terrain-data coverage and the stated scientific limitations.

Public demonstration and operational modes

The public application is deployed as a React frontend on Render with a separately hosted FastAPI backend.

The hosted backend currently operates in synthetic/mock mode because the real HiRISE DTM is not mounted in that environment. Its route measurements and mission scores are therefore illustrative and must not be interpreted as real Martian terrain observations.

The local deployment can be configured with the actual HiRISE DTM for raster-backed elevation and slope analysis. NASA Solar System Treks map services require an internet connection.

Technology

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, OpenLayers and Recharts.
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI and Pydantic.
  • Geospatial processing: Rasterio, NumPy, pyproj and Shapely.
  • Deployment: Docker, Docker Compose, Nginx and Render.
  • Testing: Pytest and Playwright.
  • Version control: Git and GitHub.

Benefits and intended impact

VyomPath makes Martian terrain information easier to explore, compare and communicate. Its mission-aware evaluation helps users understand why a route may be preferable for one mission objective but not another.

By combining route geometry, terrain measurements, data coverage and explainable scoring, it turns static terrain visualization into an interactive exploration-planning experience.

The system is intended for exploration, education and preliminary decision support. It does not replace rover autonomy, ground-truth validation or mission engineering review.

Creativity and design considerations

VyomPath's central contribution is combining a two-path geospatial architecture with mission-specific, explainable traverse evaluation.

Its scoring engine is deterministic and based on documented mathematical rules rather than an opaque AI-generated recommendation. It exposes the trade-offs behind each result, treats unknown terrain explicitly and distinguishes genuine raster measurements from synthetic demonstration outputs.

The team prioritized coordinate consistency, raster validity, data provenance, reproducible analysis and honest communication of scientific limitations.

Use of Super Intelligence

Generative AI tools, including Google Antigravity, Anthropic Claude and ChatGPT, assisted with research, feature ideation, code scaffolding, debugging, test development and technical documentation.

The Mission-Aware Traverse Intelligence engine itself uses deterministic, rule-based weighted calculations. It does not embed an LLM or machine-learning model to generate route scores or recommendations. The team reviewed the implementation, testing and scientific assumptions and remains responsible for the final project and its results.
